source.title: VISOR: Visual Input-based Steering for Output Redirection in Vision-Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The paper applies CAA activation steering vectors and evaluates refusal-related behavior in VLMs, but does not test the original all-layer ablation procedure or its full set of claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports activation-level steering-vector comparisons for refusal, but Table 1 is flattened in the supplied text and the refusal values cannot be reliably assigned to model, direction, and method. Hyperparameter-search results are not outcomes. VISOR image results and MMLU performance concern the paper's new input-space method, not the direction itself, so they are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study's question is whether optimized images (VISOR) can reproduce the effect of activation steering vectors. The refusal steering vector is a CAA vector built from contrastive A/B answer pairs (refuse minus comply) in Panickssery et al.'s refusal dataset, applied at hyperparameter-searched layers. It is not the harmful-minus-harmless instruction difference-in-means direction named in V1. It serves only as a comparator for VISOR. Refusal is measured as a likelihood score (BAS) on multiple-choice answer options, not as refusal of open-ended harmful requests. No ablation, weight edit, capability check of the vector, or analysis of direction structure is done. The study uses steering as a tool and benchmarks its own input-space method against it, so it does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a single optimized image (VISOR) matches, and sometimes exceeds, CAA steering vectors in shifting sycophancy, anti-survival and refusal behavior bidirectionally in LLaVA-1.5 and Idefics2. They add that VISOR leaves MMLU performance essentially unchanged (maximum drop of 0.1%). They frame this both as a practical steering channel and as a security vulnerability that bypasses text-based defenses.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CAA steering vectors as the activation-level comparison, but the study focuses on optimized visual inputs and does not reproduce the original direction-ablation procedure.

fits_no_version.finding: In LLaVA-1.5-7B and Idefics2-8b, a CAA refusal steering vector added to activations shifts refusal-option likelihood (BAS) up and down on Panickssery's refusal A/B dataset. A single optimized image (VISOR) reproduces similar shifts, with at most 0.1% MMLU change for VISOR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastive-answer (CAA) refusal steering vectors bidirectionally shift refusal likelihood in VLMs, and their effect can be reproduced via optimized visual inputs without runtime access to model internals.

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted at the AAAI 2026 Workshop AIR-FM, Assessing and Improving Reliability of Foundation Models in the Real World.
record.problems: The refusal results in Table 1 are not reliably recoverable from the supplied flattened layout. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for these results. Its MMLU capability check is for VISOR, not for activation-vector ablation or addition.
record.rows_left_out: VISOR image steering and system-prompt results in Table 1, and VISOR MMLU results in Table 2, were left out because they do not directly test the activation direction. Other behavior categories in Table 1 were also left out because they are not refusal results.

untested.parts: Ablation of a harmful-minus-harmless direction, inducing refusal on harmless requests via that direction, and capability preservation under direction intervention.
Whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction, and adversarial training against ablation.
Transfer across languages, variants, or base/instruct models (text-to-VLM transfer is not examined).

record.verdict_notes: Arditi et al. is cited only to note that CAA has a weight-space analogue. Table 1 is flattened: behavior labels appear at the end, and the refusal numbers cannot be assigned with confidence, so no numbers are taken from it.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test ablating the direction at every layer and position, whether most refusals remain after ablation, refusal of harmless requests, or preservation of general capability under direction ablation.
Weight-editing or abliteration removal in released models.
Whether attacks suppress the direction or training against its ablation adds robustness.
Whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or distributed across multiple directions.
Whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from the refusal decision.
Transfer of the direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
How refusal-training method or timing determines whether one removable direction exists.
Whether the claim holds for reasoning models.
